strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important gap: fusing vision with proprioception and multi-contact touch for physically grounded, metric-scale 3D reconstruction under severe hand occlusion, rather than relying on vision alone.

Technically coherent pipeline: a pose-aware, camera-aligned SDF representation with a Structure-VAE latent space enables differentiable physics objectives (contact-consistency and non-interpenetration) to be used both as finetuning losses and as decoder-guided control terms at inference time.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental protocol: comparisons against two representative recent baselines (Amodal3R, SAM3D) across multiple occlusion bins and multiple metrics for both reconstruction and pose estimation.
Useful ablations isolating the contribution of proprioception vs. touch, and studying robustness to tactile localization noise, which support the claimed design choices.

Real-world deployment on a humanoid robot with an end-effector unseen during training is a valuable, uncommon validation step that strengthens claims of practical applicability and cross-embodiment transfer.
Extensive supplementary material detailing data generation, grid canonicalization, and real-world calibration procedures aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core architecture largely reuses existing components (TRELLIS/SLAT-style flow transformers, Amodal3R-style occlusion conditioning), with the main contribution being the addition of touch/proprioception conditioning and physics-based losses/guidance rather than a fundamentally new representation or algorithm.

Baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: SAM3D is evaluated with ground-truth depth for pose estimation and has larger model/data capacity, while Amodal3R lacks any interaction signal by design, making the improvement attribution partly expected rather than a controlled comparison.

Real-world results are less convincing than simulation: Table 3 shows the proposed method is only marginally better or comparable to SAM3D on several metrics (e.g., worse F@0.02), and the qualitative real examples show visible hand-object misalignment artifacts due to calibration noise.
Real-world evaluation is limited in scale (5 objects, one end-effector, no repeated trials/statistics), limiting confidence in generalization claims beyond the tested setup.

The method's reliance on accurate camera-hand extrinsics, forward kinematics, and reliable occluder/visibility masks is a significant practical dependency, and errors in these (explicitly acknowledged) can bias reconstructions, restricting real-world robustness.

Fixed 64^3 grid resolution constrains fidelity for thin structures/concavities, and this limitation is compounded in manipulation scenes since hand and object share the same grid, reducing effective object resolution.

No variance/uncertainty reporting across seeds or trials for the quantitative tables, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported improvements, especially the smaller margins in less occluded bins.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap: fusing proprioception and multi-contact tactile signals as explicit geometric constraints for occlusion-aware 3D generative reconstruction, rather than relying on vision alone.

The pose-aware, camera-aligned SDF representation is a clean design choice that enables consistent alignment between 2D evidence, hand geometry, and tactile contacts in a shared 3D grid, and supports differentiable physics-based losses/guidance.

The two-stage pipeline (Structure-VAE + flow-matching pretraining/finetuning, physics-aware losses, decoder-based inference-time guidance) is technically well thought out, with clear formulations (Eikonal/normal regularization, non-interpenetration and contact-consistency losses, EMA-guided control term).

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: stratified results by occlusion level, comparison to two relevant and fairly strong baselines (Amodal3R, SAM3D), pose-estimation evaluation, and both simulation and real-world experiments.
Real-robot deployment with an end-effector unseen during training demonstrates meaningful cross-embodiment transfer, which is a nontrivial and practically relevant validation beyond simulation.
Extensive ablations (sensing modality ablation, tactile noise robustness, calibration-error discussion) and detailed supplementary material aid reproducibility and support the paper's claims.
Honest discussion of limitations (calibration dependency, fixed-grid resolution, generalization to different hands/sensor layouts) strengthens the credibility of the claims.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are somewhat confounded: SAM3D uses a larger model and more training data, and for pose estimation SAM3D is given an advantage (GT depth) while the proposed method leverages privileged proprioceptive/tactile information not available to baselines, making the comparison more illustrative than strictly controlled.

No quantitative comparison against prior vision+touch fusion methods (e.g., TouchSDF, Smith et al. vision-and-touch reconstruction) that are directly related in spirit; only vision-only baselines are benchmarked, leaving the added value of touch relative to other tactile-fusion approaches unclear.

Real-world quantitative evaluation is limited in scale (5 objects, one robot platform, one grasp per trial description), and the method actually underperforms SAM3D on F@0.02 in this setting, with gains generally more modest than in simulation.

The overall reconstruction metrics (Table 1, "All") show only moderate improvement over SAM3D despite the substantially higher sensing/infrastructure requirements (tactile hardware, calibrated proprioception), raising questions about the practical cost-benefit tradeoff.

The physics-guidance mechanism at inference (EMA update, trust region, gradient normalization) relies on several heuristic stabilization choices that are not individually ablated, making it hard to assess which components are essential.
No discussion of computational overhead/inference latency introduced by the multi-stream conditioning, physics losses, and decoder-guided sampling, which is relevant for robotics deployment.

Grasp data generation depends on a specific pretrained grasp-synthesis model and is restricted to object scales compatible with that model, which may limit generalization to more diverse object geometries and sizes not explicitly tested.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-explored gap: fusing proprioception and multi-contact touch as explicit geometric constraints for occlusion-aware 3D generative reconstruction, rather than relying on vision alone.

Technically well-designed pipeline: a pose-aware, camera-aligned SDF representation combined with a Structure-VAE latent space and conditional flow matching, with physically motivated contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses used both in training and as inference-time guidance.

Comprehensive experimental validation: simulation benchmarks against two representative baselines (Amodal3R, SAM3D) stratified by occlusion level, pose-estimation evaluation, and an extensive ablation study isolating the contribution of each sensing modality, noise robustness, and each architectural/training component.

Real-world validation on a humanoid robot with an end-effector unseen during training demonstrates practical cross-embodiment transfer, which is a meaningful and rarely-shown result for this class of methods.

Additional comparisons with specialized human-hand reconstruction methods (EasyHOI, FollowMyHold) in the supplementary material, showing competitive accuracy at drastically lower inference time and near-perfect reconstruction rate.

Honest and specific limitations/discussion (dependency on calibration, fixed-resolution grid, seed sensitivity, camera-aligned vs. object-centric frame trade-offs) that clarify the scope of claims rather than overselling.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: Amodal3R and SAM3D are trained on larger/different datasets and (for SAM3D) with larger model capacity, and SAM3D's pose baseline is additionally given ground-truth depth, which muddies the isolation of the proposed multimodal-physics contribution as the sole source of improvement.

Real-world evaluation is limited in scale (5 objects, single robot platform) and shows only marginal or mixed improvement over SAM3D on some metrics (e.g., F@0.02 is worse than SAM3D in real-world), suggesting the benefits are more pronounced in simulation than in practice.

The method's reliance on accurate camera–hand extrinsics, forward kinematics, and visibility masks is a significant practical bottleneck; the paper shows sensitivity to kinematic noise is non-negligible, which could limit real-world applicability outside carefully calibrated setups.

Fixed 64^3 grid resolution, shared between hand and object, is acknowledged to hurt fidelity for thin structures/concavities, and this could disproportionately affect small manipulable objects relevant to robotics.

Finetuning/testing on synthetic grasps generated by one grasp-synthesis model (with objects size-matched to that model) may introduce dataset-specific biases (grasp diversity, contact distribution) that are not stress-tested against alternative grasp generators.

Some reported gains are modest in low-occlusion regimes (vision-only baseline can match or exceed the proposed method there), somewhat narrowing the claimed universal advantage of the physically grounded approach.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: exploiting proprioception and multi-contact tactile feedback as explicit geometric constraints for 3D reconstruction under hand occlusion is a meaningful gap in the literature, which is dominated by vision-only occlusion-aware generation methods.

Technically sound and clearly described pipeline: pose-aware camera-aligned SDF representation, Structure-VAE with Eikonal/normal regularization, conditional flow-matching model with pretraining/finetuning stages, and physically motivated contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses used both as training objectives and as decoder-guided sampling terms. The architecture and math are presented in good detail, aiding reproducibility.

Comprehensive experimental validation: results span simulation (with occlusion-stratified bins), real-world deployment on a humanoid robot with an unseen end-effector, and a DexYCB comparison against human-hand-specific baselines ([2],[39]) despite domain mismatch, showing competitive reconstruction rate and quality.

Thorough ablation study isolating sensing modalities (vision-only, no-touch), robustness to input noise (mask, kinematic, tactile), and model components (guidance, physics losses, contact representation type), which convincingly supports the individual contribution of each proposed component.
Cross-embodiment generalization is explicitly tested (training end-effectors differ from the real robot's), which is a valuable and non-trivial demonstration of practical applicability.
Honest discussion of limitations (calibration/pose sensitivity, fixed grid resolution, camera-aligned vs. object-centric frame) that appropriately contextualizes the claims rather than overselling.
weaknesses: The real-world experiment is limited in scale (5 objects, one embodiment, no dedicated ablation isolating vision vs. touch vs. proprioception contributions on real hardware), so the strength of the sim-to-real claim is somewhat constrained; the reported improvement over SAM3D in the real setting is marginal on several metrics (e.g., F@0.02 is worse than SAM3D).

Baselines (Amodal3R, SAM3D) are vision-only and not designed to leverage touch/proprioception, making the comparison somewhat unbalanced in favor of the proposed method; a more informative comparison might include a vision+depth or vision+proprioception baseline that does not use the same architecture family to strengthen the claim that gains come from physical grounding rather than architecture/training-data differences.

F@0.02 is not improved by the proposed method relative to SAM3D in the least-occluded bin and even in the aggregate 'All' row in Table 1 (SAM3D 0.228 vs Ours 0.189), which the paper acknowledges but does not deeply analyze; a clearer explanation of why fine-grained surface metrics sometimes favor the baseline would strengthen the paper.

Pose estimation comparison against SAM3D uses ground-truth depth for the baseline's best case, which is a somewhat favorable setup for the proposed method; a more apples-to-apples comparison (e.g., with realistic/noisy depth for SAM3D) would make the pose estimation gains more convincing.

The method depends heavily on accurate calibration (camera-hand extrinsics, forward kinematics) and a fixed 64^3 grid resolution shared between hand and object, which the authors note reduces effective object resolution in manipulation scenes; the practical impact of this on fine geometric detail (e.g., thin structures) is not quantitatively assessed beyond qualitative discussion.

Reproducibility relies on several closed or complex components (grasp-synthesis model [71], SLat pipeline adapted from [75], SAM3D refinement) and large-scale training data mixtures (3D-FUTURE, HSSD, ABO, ObjaverseXL subset, GSO) that are not all standard or trivially reproducible from the paper alone; code/data release is not explicitly promised in the manuscript excerpt provided.
